posts.title: How Often Should You Train BJJ? (And How Much Is Too Much?)
posts.description: The honest answer to how many times a week you should train BJJ depends on your age, goals, recovery capacity, and injury history. Here's the real breakdown.
posts.lede: When I started BJJ, I trained 6 days a week. I was convinced that more was better. Within 3 months, I had tendinitis in both elbows, a shoulder that clicked every time I raised my arm, and a lower back that hurt when I sat down. I learned the hard way that more isn't better. Better is better.

content.text: The Short Answer

For most people: 3-4 sessions per week is the sweet spot. Enough to make consistent progress. Enough recovery time to avoid injury and burnout. Less than 3 and progress is slow. More than 5 and injury risk rises significantly unless you're young, well-recovered, and built for it.
By Experience Level
White Belt: 2-3x/week

Your body is adapting to a sport it's never done before. The connective tissue (ligaments, tendons) takes 6-12 months to strengthen. Training more than 3x/week as a beginner increases injury risk without proportional skill gain.
Blue Belt: 3-4x/week
Your body has adapted. You can handle more volume. 4 sessions is where most blue belts start making real progress.
Purple Belt and Above: 3-5x/week
At purple belt and beyond, you know your body well enough to manage volume. Many advanced grapplers train 4-5x/week but at varying intensities — some hard rounds, some flow rounds.
By Age Group
Under 25: 4-5x/week
Recovery is fast. Connective tissue is resilient. This is the only age bracket where 5+ sessions is sustainable.
Recovery starts to slow. Work and life add stress. 3-4 quality sessions beat 6 mediocre, injury-prone sessions.
This is the sweet spot for longevity. I'm 40 and I train 3x/week with one competition prep block per year where I bump to 4. My 3 sessions are better quality than my 6 sessions at 25.
45+: 2-3x/week + mobility work
Quality over quantity. Add daily mobility work on off-days. At this stage, consistency over decades beats intensity over months.
Signs You're Training Too Much

items: Your joints hurt in the morning (not muscle soreness — joint pain)
You're irritable or depressed without obvious cause
Your sleep quality has dropped
You're getting sick more often
Your BJJ feels 'stuck' or frustrating
You don't look forward to training

content.text: My rule: If you woke up today and don't want to train, don't train. Take the day off. Do mobility work instead. The mats will be there tomorrow. Your body's willingness to train is the most accurate indicator of whether you need rest.

faq.q: Is 4 times a week enough for BJJ?
faq.a: Yes. 4 sessions per week is ideal for most intermediate and advanced grapplers. You'll make steady progress with adequate recovery.

faq.q: Can I train BJJ every day?
faq.a: You can, but you shouldn't — at least not at full intensity. Professional competitors train 5-6 days but periodize intensity. For recreational grapplers, daily training leads to burnout and injury within 3-6 months.

faq.q: Is 2 hours of BJJ a week enough?
faq.a: 2 hours (one session) is better than nothing, but progress will be very slow. For consistent improvement, aim for at least 3 hours per week.

faq.q: How many times a week do BJJ professionals train?
faq.a: Professional competitors typically train 5-6 days per week with 1-2 sessions per day. They also have dedicated recovery protocols, nutrition plans, and coaching support that recreational grapplers don't have.

posts.title: Is 30 Too Old to Start BJJ? (No — And Here's Why)
posts.description: The honest truth about starting BJJ at 30, 35, 40, or 50. How to train safely as an older beginner, avoid the common injuries, and actually make progress without breaking down.
posts.lede: I started BJJ at 25. By 28, my back was so bad I couldn't stand up straight. Most people would have quit. I didn't — I adapted. I learned that age isn't the problem. The problem is training like you're 20 when you're not. I'm 40 now and I roll better than I ever did at 25. Here's how.

content.text: The Truth About Starting BJJ at 30+
30 is not too old to start BJJ. Neither is 35, 40, or 50. The question isn't whether you CAN start — it's whether you're willing to train SMART.

The grapplers who thrive starting older are the ones who: do mobility work before class, tap early, train at 70% intensity, prioritize recovery, and don't ego-roll. The ones who quit are the ones who try to keep up with 22-year-olds from day one.

Real examples from my gym: Our oldest white belt started at 52. He's been training for 4 years. He doesn't roll with the competition team. He does his mobility work. He taps to everything. And he's having the time of his life. That's BJJ done right.
The Older Beginner's Training Rules

items: 10 minutes of mobility work before every class. Not optional.
Choose your training partners. Older, calmer, more technical grapplers. Avoid the spazzy white belt.
Tap early. The ego hit lasts 2 seconds. A joint injury lasts months.
Train 2-3x per week. Not more. Your connective tissue needs recovery.
Do mobility work on off days. 10 minutes. Every day.
Sleep 7+ hours. This is when your body repairs.
Eat enough protein. Muscle maintenance is harder after 30.

content.text: Is 40 Too Old to Compete in BJJ?

No. Most BJJ tournaments have Masters divisions (30+, 35+, 40+, 45+, 50+). These are some of the most competitive and technical divisions in any tournament. Masters competitors rely on technique over athleticism, which makes their matches fun to watch and safer to compete in.

faq.a: Yes. Hundreds of people start BJJ in their 40s every year. The key is training smart: mobility work, partner selection, and recovery.

faq.q: Can older adults learn BJJ effectively?
faq.a: Absolutely. Older adults often learn BJJ more effectively than younger ones because they have better patience, body awareness, and ego management.

faq.q: What belt can you get starting BJJ at 30?
faq.a: If you train consistently and avoid major injuries, you can reach black belt by your mid-40s (10-15 years). Many people earn their black belt in their 40s and 50s.
For professional MMA, 30 is late. For recreational BJJ and competition in Masters divisions, 30 is not old at all.

posts.title: Can I Build Muscle With a Herniated Disc? (Yes — Here's How I Did It)
posts.description: Building muscle with a herniated disc isn't just possible — it's essential for recovery. Here's exactly how I gained 10 pounds of muscle while rehabbing my L5-S1 herniation.
posts.lede: When the MRI showed my herniated disc, the first thing my doctor said was "no heavy lifting." I interpreted that as "no training at all." For three months, I did nothing. I got weaker. My back hurt more. Then I met a physio who specialized in athletes, and he said the opposite: "You NEED to build muscle. Your spine needs a muscular armor." He was right. I gained 10 pounds of muscle during my disc recovery. Here's exactly how.

content.text: Why Muscle Protects Your Discs

Your spine is stabilized by muscles — the deep core (transverse abdominis, multifidus), the glutes, and the back extensors. When these muscles are weak, the load of every movement — including BJJ — transfers directly to your spinal discs and joints. Building muscle around your spine creates a natural weight belt that absorbs and distributes force.
The Safe Training Protocol
Exercises I DID (Safe for Herniated Disc)

items: Dead bugs — core stability without spinal loading
Bird dogs — posterior chain + core, zero compression
Glute bridges — builds glutes that protect the lower back
Side planks — oblique strength without spinal flexion
Kettlebell swings — posterior chain power with neutral spine
Pull-ups — upper body without spinal compression
Farmer carries — core stability under load, no spinal compression
Dumbbell Romanian deadlifts — light weight, controlled, posterior chain

content.text: Exercises I AVOIDED

items: Barbell back squats — axial loading compresses discs
Conventional deadlifts — too much spinal loading during recovery
Good mornings — directly loads the lumbar spine
Sit-ups/crunches — spinal flexion under load
Leg press — compresses the spine against the pad

content.text: The 12-Week Muscle-Building Protocol
Week 1-4: Bodyweight only. Dead bugs, glute bridges, bird dogs, side planks. 3 sets of 15. Daily. Focus on mind-muscle connection.
Week 5-8: Add light resistance. Kettlebell swings (12-16kg), farmer carries (16kg per hand), pull-ups (assisted if needed). 3x/week, not daily.
Week 9-12: Progressive overload. Increase weight gradually. Kettlebell swings (20-24kg). Add dumbbell RDLs. Continue core work. You should be noticeably stronger and pain-free at this point.

faq.q: Can deadlifts cause a herniated disc?
faq.a: Improper deadlift form can cause a herniated disc. But proper deadlift form — with a braced core and neutral spine — is actually protective for the spine. The key is proper coaching and progressive loading.

faq.q: Is walking good for a herniated disc?
faq.a: Yes. Walking is excellent for disc recovery. It pumps fluid through the discs, improves circulation, and reduces inflammation. Walk 20-30 minutes daily on flat ground.

faq.q: Can I do kettlebell swings with a herniated disc?
faq.a: Yes — if your form is correct and you start light. The kettlebell swing trains the posterior chain with a neutral spine, which builds the muscular armor your discs need. Start with 12kg and progress slowly.
